title: Spotting AI Fakes
about: Spot fake reviews and bot accounts, and check claims outside the post.

cards.title: 200 five-star reviews
cards.body:
A brand-new skateboard shop opens online. By morning it has 200 five-star reviews, all calling the boards "amazing".

Real customers don't work that fast. With AI, anyone can make **fake reviews**, fake news and **bots** (accounts that post automatically) in seconds. False information that spreads is called misinformation.

cards.prompt: Fake reviews often look like **one source pretending to be many**. Is each sign **suspicious** or **normal**?

items.label: 50 reviews posted on the same day
Lots use the same unusual words
A mix of good and bad reviews

cards.hint: Picture real customers: do they all buy on one day and use the same words?
cards.nudge: A few bad reviews can be a good sign. Which look like many accounts acting as one?
cards.explanation: Floods of reviews, the same unusual words and reviewers with no history look like **one source pretending to be many**. Real reviews are mixed, specific and spread out.

cards.prompt: Real reviews mention **specific details**; fakes are **vague and over the top**. Does each **look real**, or **suspicious**?

items.label: 5 stars from an account made today

cards.hint: Could the review be written without ever touching the product?
cards.nudge: A complaint doesn't make a review fake. Which say nothing only a real user would know?
cards.explanation: Real reviews mention **specific details**, even when happy. Gushing words with no details, and brand-new accounts, are warning signs: clues, not proof.

cards.prompt: Shocking posts get shared before they're checked, and fakes look polished. Is each check **outside** the post, or **inside**?

items.label: Look for it on trusted news
Find out who runs the account
Check how sharp the photos are

cards.hint: Does the check need a new tab, or just the post in front of you?
cards.nudge: Fakes can look polished and sharp. Which checks learn about it from somewhere else?
cards.explanation: Searching, trusted news and finding who's behind it look **outside** the post. Re-reading, polish and photo quality only look **inside**, where good fakes pass easily.

cards.prompt: All four of these are fake. Which one is **most likely** to be shared before anyone checks it?

options.text: A made-up report on last year's local rainfall
options.nudge: It's fake, but does it make anyone feel much? What makes people share fast?

options.text: A wrong list of the local library's opening hours
options.nudge: That's annoying, but would people rush to share it? Think about strong feelings.

options.text: "SHOCKING: our local park is being bulldozed!"
A fake banana bread recipe with a "secret" ingredient
options.nudge: Mildly interesting, but it doesn't make people feel much. Which one would?

cards.hint: Which one makes people feel the strongest thing, fast?
cards.explanation: The **shocking** one: shock and anger make people share first and check later. So a strong feeling is your cue to stop.

cards.prompt: A site you've never heard of says chocolate cures colds, quoting "Dr Sam Lee, a top scientist". Best first move?

options.text: Read the whole article slowly to look for mistakes
options.nudge: AI-written fakes often have no mistakes. Check inside the article, or outside it?

options.text: Check it quotes a scientist, so an expert backs it
options.nudge: Quotes are easy to invent, and "Dr Sam Lee" may not exist. How could you check outside?

options.text: Search the claim and the site's name in another tab
Read the comments to see if most people agree
options.nudge: Comments can be fake, and agreement isn't evidence. Where else could you look?

cards.hint: Look back at where to check: inside the post, or outside it?
cards.explanation: **Search outside the article** for the claim, the site and the "expert". AI fakes can be polished, quote invented people and fill the comments.

cards.prompt: Under a video about a new game, an account replies to dozens of comments within a minute.

steps.text: Every reply says almost the same: "This game is a SCAM, download SuperBlast instead!!" with a link. What's going on?

choices.text: A real fan of SuperBlast who wants others to try it
choices.consequence: One person can't post dozens of near-identical replies in a minute. That's automatic.

choices.text: A bot posting automatically to push that link
choices.consequence: Yes: speed, copy-paste replies and a link are classic bot signs. Don't click it, and report it.

choices.text: A real, honest warning that the game is a scam
choices.consequence: A real warning wouldn't be copied into dozens of replies linking another game. That's a bot advertising.

cards.hint: Think about the speed, the sameness, and what it wants you to do.
cards.explanation: Dozens of near-identical replies in a minute, all with the same link, is a **bot**. Don't click, and use the report button.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- AI makes fake reviews, articles and bots fast and cheap.
- Warning signs: floods at once, vague gushing, brand-new accounts.
- Strong feeling? Stop, and check **outside** the post.

Next: keeping your private stuff private.
